supplement.where: Appendix A, cited for the prompt templates on PDF p. 3 (printed p. 1099), Section II.B. The appendix is not in this PDF, and the paper gives no URL.
supplement.holds: The text identifies standardized prompt templates as the contents of Appendix A. It does not state that supplementary statistics are provided; the appendix itself is absent from the saved PDF.

paper_design_summary: The paper describes short film scripts (one scene per premise) on matched premises in four genres (drama, thriller, comedy, sci-fi) under three authorship conditions: written by professional screenwriters (human-only), generated in one pass by a GPT-series model (AI-minimal), or generated by the model and refined over up to five rounds of critiques from a human editor (iterative human-AI). Industry screenwriters, script editors, and development executives scored the anonymized scripts blind on an adapted script-coverage rubric, and the paper describes one-way ANOVA with post-hoc tests (PDF pp. 2-3, Sections II.A-E; p. 6, Section IV). The setup is described as a simulation; no allocation of writers or editors to conditions is reported, and no scripts, writers, editors, or evaluators are counted.

studies.label: Premise-matched screenplay corpus scored blind by industry experts (human-only vs AI-minimal vs iterative human-AI)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Each matched premise and genre was rendered under all three authorship conditions (human-only, AI-minimal, iterative human-AI). The reported source of variation is the script-generation branch; no allocation or randomization of people is described. The within structure refers to matched premises, not a reported randomized within-person order.
assignment.quote: Proposed mixed-methods workflow (see Fig. 1) model uses matched conditions of genre and premise in 3 parallel branches: human-only, AI-minimal intervention and iterative human-AI collaboration.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 2 (printed p. 1098), Section I.D; also Section II.A ('Started three parallel branches on every premise Pj and on every genre Gk') and Eq. 1

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Scripts written by professional screenwriters with no AI involvement ('pure professional authorship', Section II.A).

arms.name: AI-minimal
arms.description: Script generated by a GPT-series model in one pass from a standardized prompt and the premise, with minimal human editing (Eq. 2).

arms.name: Iterative Human-AI
arms.description: GPT-series draft refined by the model over up to five feedback-refinement iterations in which a human editor supplies qualitative critiques (Eq. 3).

participants.exclusions: Not stated. The paper reports no number of scripts, premises, screenwriters, human editors, or evaluators. It says only that the dataset 'consists of the same numbers of screenplays per condition' (PDF p. 3, Section II.E) and lists a 'Moderate sample size of evaluators' as a limitation (PDF p. 6, Section IV).
participants.who: Professional screenwriters wrote the human-only scripts. A human editor ('the human editors' in Section III.B), number not stated, gave critiques in the iterative condition. Screenwriters, script editors, and development executives working in the industry scored the scripts. No group is counted.
participants.quote: Human-only scripts were written by professional screenwriters. The following scripts were generated using an AI model with minimal editing: Up to five feedback-refinement iterations were conducted with a human editor for each of the iterative human-AI scripts.
participants.locator: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 1099), Section II.B; evaluators in Section II.D; 'Moderate sample size of evaluators' in Section IV, PDF p. 6 (printed p. 1102)

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-series large language models via a cloud-based inference engine (specific model not stated)
ai_tool.how_used: The model writes the whole script. AI-minimal: one-pass generation, s_min = LLM(I, P_j) (Eq. 2). Iterative: the model writes a draft and refines it from a human editor's critiques, s_t+1 = LLM_refine(s_t, F_t), up to five iterations (Eq. 3 and the pseudocode, PDF p. 3). In the pseudocode the human editor reviews and comments, and the model rewrites.

task.description: Short film scripts, one scene per premise, on matched premises in four genres: drama, thriller, comedy, sci-fi.
task.duration: Not stated for any session. Table 5 (caption: hypothetical LLM backend) lists human effort per script of 120 min (human-only), 5 min (AI-minimal), and 25 min (iterative human-AI); Section IV calls the effort metrics hypothetical (PDF p. 5, Table 5; p. 6, Section IV).

outcomes.name: Overall Average rubric score (Table 1)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Blind scoring by industry screenwriters, script editors, and development executives on an adapted professional script-coverage rubric. Eq. 4 defines the overall rubric score R as a weighted sum of four measures (thematic complexity and emotional resonance combined in M_tc; weights not given), but Table 1 prints five metric rows and an Overall Average, and the paper never says the two are the same (PDF p. 3, Section II.D; p. 4, Table 1). The rating scale is not stated. Robustness variants are grouped here: overall scores by genre (Table 2), by collaboration iterations (Table 3), and by prompt refinement depth (Table 4), all on PDF p. 5. The paper does not separately identify the raters or script sets for Tables 3-4; expert_raters follows the general evaluation description in Section II.D.

company_involvement.description: No company role in the study, funding statement, or acknowledgment is printed. Both authors list company affiliations: Zero Density Inc, USA (Hukerikar, Technical Account Manager) and CapitalOne Bank, USA (Singavarapu, Senior Data Analyst/Engineer). The AI is described only as GPT-series models on a cloud-based inference engine; no AI company is named.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 1097), author block; PDF p. 3, Sections II.B and II.E

eligibility.reason: The reported design compares scripts produced through matched authorship branches, with no reported random assignment of people to AI assistance or randomized within-person order; it therefore does not meet criterion 1 (PDF p. 2, Sections I.D and II.A, Figures 1-2; p. 3, Sections II.B-C). No number of distinct writers or editors analyzed is given, so the 50-person threshold cannot be verified; unreported script and evaluator counts cannot substitute for creative-task participants (PDF p. 3, Sections II.B and II.E; p. 6, Section IV). Criterion 3 is met on the reported method: the level of creative output was measured using a script-coverage rubric, with blind judging by industry screenwriters, script editors, and development executives (PDF p. 3, Section II.D; scores in p. 4, Table 1). Retain ai_vs_human as the context classification for this script-corpus comparison. Whether the iterative editor branch is instead described as a non-random human-AI comparison does not establish random assignment. The empirical status of the scripts and ratings remains an author-clarification item; the current criterion-3 decision follows the explicit evaluation description.

one_line_finding: Blind industry experts gave scripts an Overall Average rubric score of 8.42 when professional screenwriters wrote them, 6.26 when a GPT-series model generated them in one pass, and 8.20 when the model refined them from a human editor's critiques; one-pass scripts scored 8.9 vs 8.7 on narrative coherence (n.s.) but 4.8 vs 8.5 on thematic complexity (p < 0.05), and the paper prints means and significance marks only, with no SDs or counts (PDF p. 4, Table 1 and Section III.A).
open_questions: Design class: in the iterative arm a human editor directs the model, so iterative vs human-only resembles people working with and without AI under non-random assignment (quasi_people). Both screeners and the reconciler keep ai_vs_human, because no person is assigned or counted, the model writes every script in the two AI arms, and the paper frames the work as a simulation that compares authorship conditions.

Are the scripts and ratings real? The paper calls the setup a 'controlled simulation environment' and a 'virtual setting', Table 5 is labeled 'hypothetical LLM backend', and Section IV calls the effort metrics hypothetical. Table 1 column headers cite references [13] and [14], and Table 2 headers cite [15] and [16]; [14] is a paper on video grounding. The paper does not say whether the scores are its own data.

Construct: the rubric is a script-coverage quality rubric that the paper calls a measure of creative output. The final form codes the overall score overall_creativity, narrative coherence usefulness, and the other four components other. A reviewer may prefer usefulness for the overall score.

Direction without a pairwise test: for iterative vs human-only, S1-O1 and S1-O6 follow the paper's own statements ('very similar', 'nearly matched') and S1-O3 to S1-O5 follow the printed means, as earlier reconciled forms do (c018 for the first rule, c094 and c158 for the second). A reviewer may prefer one rule for all five.
notes: The paper reports no number of premises, scripts, writers, editors, or evaluators, no explicit rating-scale range, and no SDs, SEs, or numerical test statistics. Table 1 gives means and one significance column (* or n.s.); Section II.D describes one-way ANOVA and post-hoc tests with p < 0.05 as the threshold (PDF p. 3). The single marker for a row is not assigned to specific pairwise comparisons. Section III.A explicitly describes significant AI-minimal versus human-only differences for character depth and thematic complexity, and significant iterative improvements without naming the comparison arm in that p-value sentence (PDF p. 4). Availability codes p_value_only retain this limited significance reporting and do not imply that each contrast has its own reported test. The unit of analysis is not stated: output (script) remains the working value, and the paper does not say whether ratings were averaged across evaluators. Internal reporting inconsistencies: Eq. 4 has four weighted measures with unstated weights, while Table 1 lists five components and an Overall Average; the relationship is not specified (PDF pp. 3-4). Section III.C says iterative scores exceeded AI-minimal by 1.5 to 1.9 points in Thriller and Sci-Fi, while Table 2 prints Thriller 8.1 versus 6.8 (PDF p. 5). Tables 3 and 4 use different refinement settings (1, 3, 5 iterations and 0, 2, 4+ edits), and the paper does not say how either relates to the main Table 1 arms (PDF p. 5). The text refers to Table 4 for runtime data printed in Table 5 and to Figure 4 for iteration scores; Figure 5 has two captions and plots overall score and percentage improvement by condition, despite its lower caption referring to collaboration iterations (PDF pp. 4-5). Section III.C names an undefined SAFL framework. Table 1 and Table 2 headers cite references [13] to [16], including a video-grounding paper at [14], leaving score provenance unclear (PDF pp. 4-5 and 7). Not separately coded as outcomes: Table 5 and Figure 6, which concern hypothetical effort/runtime; Figures 3-4, which display Table 1 means; Figure 5; and the qualitative thematic analysis of evaluator feedback (PDF pp. 4-6). Limitations stated in Section IV include short film scripts (one scene per premise), a virtual setting, a moderate evaluator sample without a count, and hypothetical effort metrics (PDF p. 6). Finalization: the entire markdown and all PDF pages were read, and Tables 1-5 were extracted directly from the PDF. No c070 challenge files were present. To follow the current spec, the former S1-O7 robustness results are grouped by construct into S1-O1, S1-O3, and S1-O5; all their printed scores are retained. Descriptions of significance markers were narrowed to what the source states, unprinted arithmetic summaries were removed from the active extraction, and eligibility reasons received explicit locators. The reconciliation object remains unchanged as the record of the earlier review; challenge-resolution counts cover challenge problems only.

open_items.item: Design subtype (open_questions[0]): retain ai_vs_human for the reported script-corpus comparison; the iterative branch includes human editorial feedback, so a non-random human-AI description is also defensible. Neither description supplies random assignment of people or randomized within-person order. This context-label boundary does not change the criterion-1 failure of the reported design (PDF pp. 2-3, Sections II.A-C and Figure 2). No further source is needed for the current exclusion.

Empirical status of scripts and ratings (open_questions[1]): Section II.D-E reports blind expert judging, but the paper also describes a simulation and a virtual setting; only the effort metrics are explicitly called hypothetical (PDF pp. 2-3 and 6). Authors should confirm that the scores in Tables 1-4 are observed human judgments on actual scripts and explain the references in the table headers (PDF pp. 4-5 and 7). This bears on criterion 3 and the existence of a human sample. Criterion 3 is met on the stated evaluation method unless that account is clarified otherwise.

Construct mapping (open_questions[2]): retain overall_creativity for the overall score because Section II.D explicitly describes measuring creative output with the adapted rubric; retain usefulness for narrative coherence and other for the remaining rubric components (PDF pp. 3-4). Choosing usefulness for the overall script-quality score would not change its status as an output-based evaluation on a creative task. No additional source is required for eligibility.

Direction and absent pairwise tests (open_questions[3]): retain the source-based descriptive convention, using the authors' similarity statements for overall score and emotional resonance and the printed mean ordering for character depth, dialogue authenticity, and thematic complexity (PDF p. 4, Table 1 and Sections III.A-B). The revised reporting explicitly avoids assigning row-level significance markers to specific pairs; no_clear_difference does not establish equivalence. This reporting choice affects no eligibility criterion and requires no further source for screening.

Number of distinct creative-task participants analyzed: writers and human editors are described but never counted (PDF p. 3, Sections II.B and II.E; p. 6, Section IV). Authors would need to provide the number of distinct people analyzed across the conditions and any exclusions to settle criterion 2. Script, rating, and evaluator counts cannot establish the 50-participant threshold.

Missing Appendix A: the paper cites it for standardized prompt templates (PDF p. 3, Section II.B), but it is absent from the saved seven-page PDF and no location is supplied. The supplement would settle the prompt-template details. No statistics, assignment details, or participant counts are stated to be located there; its absence does not change the current eligibility decision.
